source.title: Find the Maximum Number of Marked Indices

teaching.hint: If a pairing is possible, can its smaller members be replaced by even smaller available values?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: A feasible k-pair matching can be transformed into the k smallest values paired in sorted order with the k largest values.
solution_outline.approach: Sort values. Scan candidate small values from the beginning and partner values from the upper half starting at ceil(n/2). Pair the smallest unpaired candidate with the first partner meeting its doubled threshold; discard partners that are too small. Return twice the pair count.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: Chosen pairs are disjoint. The next candidate is the smallest unpaired lower-half value, and skipped partners cannot serve it or any larger candidate.
solution_outline.correctness: Uncrossing sorted small/large matches preserves threshold feasibility. Replacing the smaller members by the k smallest inputs and partners by the k largest only eases every inequality; these sets are disjoint for k<=floor(n/2). Thus the two halves contain an optimal matching. A too-small partner can serve no remaining candidate; taking the smallest feasible partner can be exchanged into an optimum without hurting later larger partners. The scan therefore attains the maximum pair count.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(log n) auxiliary sorting stack space for an in-place comparison sort.
solution_outline.pitfall: A value must not be consumed early as a small partner if that destroys the separate low/high matching roles; count marked indices, not pairs.

common_wrong_turns: A value must not be consumed early as a small partner if that destroys the separate low/high matching roles; count marked indices, not pairs.
source_fidelity_notes: Preserved independent index order, positive values, inequality, and one-use indices; used the sound chosen half split without repeating the canonical false floor-split claim.
